title: Fed holds rates at 3.5%-3.75% amid hawkish dissent; dot plot lifts 2026 outlook
content: The Fed's FOMC voted 9-3 on 29 July to hold its target rate at 3.50%-3.75%, with three regional presidents (Hammack, Kashkari, Logan) dissenting in favour of a hike, citing inflation persistently above the 2% target. Officials' updated dot plot lifted the expected year-end 2026 range to 3.6%-4.1% from 3.25%-3.75% previously, with markets now pricing two 25bp hikes, in September and December. Equities sold off on the hawkish shift: the Dow fell around 1.5%, while the S&P 500 and Nasdaq slid roughly 0.6%. The 10-year UST yield rose 5bp to 4.657% and the 30-year climbed over 9bp to 5.193%, steepening the curve as short-dated yields eased.

title: Brent surges above $90 as US-Iran conflict reignites, on track for ~20% July gain
content: Oil prices swung sharply through the week as US-Iran hostilities resumed. Brent fell 8.7% to $88.36/bbl and WTI dropped 7.5% to $82.61 on 27 July after Iran signalled a pause in attacks, but prices reversed once Washington reported intercepting an Iranian strike and President Trump threatened retaliation. By 29 July, Brent had rallied 7.9% to $90.74 and WTI 6.6% to $84.46, leaving Brent on track for a monthly gain of more than 20%, its best month in over two years. The volatility underscores renewed geopolitical risk to Middle East energy supply and adds to inflation concerns ahead of central bank decisions.

title: Eurozone GDP growth accelerates to 0.4% in Q2, beating forecasts
content: Eurostat's preliminary flash estimate, published 30 July, showed euro area GDP rose 0.4% quarter-on-quarter in Q2 2026 (0.5% across the EU), comfortably beating consensus forecasts of around 0.2% and marking the bloc's strongest quarterly growth in a year. Annual growth reached 1.0% in the euro area and 1.2% in the EU. Germany, France and Italy each grew 0.2% q/q, while Spain outperformed with 0.7% growth, aided partly by resilience to the oil-price shock from Middle East tensions. Consumer spending, government investment and business activity offset ongoing geopolitical and energy headwinds, adding to the case that the ECB has room to hold rates steady near-term.
